newsitem.title: SPAIN: Divided NATO leaders gather for expansion summit.
newsitem.headline: Divided NATO leaders gather for expansion summit.

text.p: NATO leaders gathered in Madrid on Monday for a summit to inaugurate a new European security order divided over how many former communist enemies to invite to join the most powerful military alliance ever assembled.

Only a day before the start of the historic meeting sealing the West's Cold War victory, the United States and a majority of its European allies remained deeply split over U.S. insistence on limiting enlargement to Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic.

President Bill Clinton, one of the first to arrive for the July 8-9 summit in the Spanish capital, has said only the three leading contenders out of 12 applicants were politically and economically ready to assume the burdens of membership.

France and Italy, backed by seven other European allies, want Slovenia and Romania included, as a reward for progress in establishing democracies and market economies and to project stability to the edge of the Black Sea and Balkan danger zones.

NATO officials said the argument, which goes to the heart of the justification for enlarging the West's defence shield into central and eastern Europe, would not be allowed to wreck the summit, but would not be resolved until the last moment.
"The heads of government are going to have a really serious discussion on their hands... we are going to go to the wire on this one," a senior alliance diplomat said.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen predicted on Monday that NATO leaders would reach agreement easily and initially limit the invitations to the three former Warsaw Pact foes.

"I don't expect it to be very tough or contentious," Cohen told reporters ahead of the two-day meeting which will also endorse closer ties with unsuccessful applicants and new cooperative relations with Russia and Ukraine.

Clinton, who has made alliance expansion the foreign policy centrepiece of his presidency, flew into Madrid's military airport after a weekend relaxing with King Juan Carlos on the Spanish holiday island of Majorca.

Keenly aware of mounting domestic opposition to the plan, which has to be ratified by the Republican-led Congress, Clinton has ruled out any compromise, angering Europeans sensitive to charges they are mere spectators at a U.S.-run NATO show.
Underlining the small amount of room he has for manoeuvre, a pre-summit editorial in the New York Times questioned the wisdom of the policy and its potential cost:
"Given the absence of a clear threat to Europe and the possibility of so many unpredictable consequences, NATO expansion seems a gratuitous risk."

Clinton was due to hold talks with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana later on Monday while alliance foreign ministers planned to debate the issue over dinner.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi signalled on Monday the debate would be lively -- a rare event for NATO summits where the most delicate issues are normally settled in advance.
"Europe cannot be denied its views on problems in its own region," he told the International Herald Tribune, urging Clinton to bow to European judgement in the matter.

"We should not forget that ethnic rivalry inside Romania was one of our nightmares regarding the future of Eastern Europe, and they have resolved the issue," he added, saying Italy would stick to its position.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright reiterated Washington's stand, but again pledged the door would remain open and another summit be held before too long, to review the cases of those left out on this occasion.
"Our principle, our position on enlargement is that we believe that at this time three countries are ready for invitations," she told reporters, adding:
"And at the same time we remain committed to an open door policy, and therefore a summit, the next summit would be an appropriate time to review other candidates."

The United States is not alone. Denmark and other Scandinavian countries have made clear they would oppose a wider enlargement if it did not include the three Baltic States -- Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.

Russia, which signed an agreement with NATO on a new partnership in May effectively agreeing to a limited enlargement, vehemently opposes membership for the former Soviet republics on its western flank.
Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs sent a letter to Solana on Monday urging him to send a clear signal NATO's doors would remain open for the Baltic states after Madrid.
U.S. officials said they were braced for a blast from President Jacques Chirac who has also said Paris' conditions for rejoining NATO's military wing have not yet been met.
Chirac's spokesman said last week, however, that Paris would not "take hostage" the leading three countries about which all agreed, just to press for the inclusion of Romania and Slovenia.
